longQuestions: Tax revenue: (1) Income tax and corporation tax — the largest direct tax; (2) Sales tax/General Sales Tax (GST) — the largest single source; (3) Customs duties on imports and exports; (4) Federal excise duty on industrial goods and services; (5) Capital value tax, withholding taxes, petroleum levy.

Non-tax revenue: (1) Profits of the State Bank and public enterprises (PTCL, OGDCL, PIA dividends); (2) Interest on loans to provinces and public corporations; (3) Fees, fines and charges — passports, licences, telecom licences; (4) Income of railways and post offices; (5) Gas development surcharge and royalties on oil and gas.

Capital receipts: internal borrowing (national savings schemes, treasury bills, Pakistan Investment Bonds), external loans and grants (IMF, World Bank, ADB, friendly countries), privatisation proceeds, and deficit financing.

Pakistan's tax system: federal taxes (income tax, sales tax, customs, federal excise) are collected by the Federal Board of Revenue; provinces collect agricultural income tax, property tax, stamp duty, motor vehicle tax, sales tax on services and abiana.

Features/weaknesses: (1) Narrow tax base — a very small part of the population files returns; (2) Low tax-to-GDP ratio (about 9–11%); (3) Heavy reliance on indirect taxes (about 60–70%), which is regressive; (4) Large-scale tax evasion and undocumented economy; (5) Exemptions for influential sectors; (6) Agriculture and retail trade are under-taxed.

(7) Complicated and frequently changing laws; (8) Weak administration and corruption; (9) Withholding taxes form a large part of direct taxes; (10) Reforms — GST, universal self-assessment, computerisation, NTN registration and the Active Taxpayers List — have been introduced but more improvement is needed.

(1) Widen the tax base by bringing all earners, including big landlords, traders and professionals, into the tax net; (2) Use NADRA and bank data to identify non-filers; (3) Reduce dependence on indirect taxes and increase the share of direct taxes; (4) Simplify the laws and make them stable; reduce rates but remove exemptions.

(5) Computerise and automate tax administration; e-filing and e-payment; (6) Train and adequately pay tax officials; strict accountability for corruption; (7) Document the economy — encourage banking transactions and discourage cash dealings; (8) Develop a tax culture by awareness campaigns and by spending revenue honestly on public services.

(9) Increase non-tax revenue through efficient public enterprises; (10) Control smuggling and under-invoicing; (11) Collect zakat and ushr efficiently; (12) Reduce wasteful expenditure so that taxes are not raised; (13) Improve coordination between federal and provincial revenue authorities.

(1) Mobilisation of resources — raising revenue for development and public services; (2) Economic growth — encouraging saving, investment and production through tax concessions and development spending; (3) Full employment — public works and incentives to industry.

(4) Price stability — controlling inflation and deflation through taxes, expenditure and borrowing; (5) Fair distribution of income and wealth — progressive taxes and spending on the poor; (6) Balance of payments improvement — import duties, export rebates.

(7) Reduction of the budget deficit and public debt; (8) Development of backward regions; (9) Provision of social services — education, health, housing; (10) Allocation of resources to priority sectors; (11) Establishment of a welfare state.

(1) Share in the federal divisible pool under the National Finance Commission (NFC) Award — the biggest source (more than 80% of provincial revenue), distributed mainly on the basis of population; (2) Straight transfers — royalties and development surcharges on oil and gas, excise on natural gas; (3) Grants and special grants from the federal government.

Provincial taxes: agricultural income tax, land revenue, property tax (urban immovable property), stamp duty and registration fees, motor vehicle tax, provincial excise (on liquor, etc.), entertainment tax, professional tax, sales tax on services (collected by PRA, SRB, KPRA, BRA), abiana (water rate), electricity duty.
Non-tax sources: fees of courts and educational institutions, income from forests, irrigation, provincial public enterprises, fines, and loans from the federal government and foreign agencies.

The recipients of zakat are named in the Holy Quran (At-Taubah 9:60) — eight categories: (1) Fuqara — the poor who have little; (2) Masakin — the needy who have nothing; (3) Amileen — those employed to collect and distribute zakat; (4) Muallafat-ul-Quloob — those whose hearts are to be reconciled (new Muslims).

(5) Fir-riqab — freeing slaves and captives; (6) Al-gharimeen — debtors unable to pay their debts; (7) Fi sabeelillah — in the way of Allah (jihad, religious and welfare purposes); (8) Ibn-us-sabeel — travellers in need, away from home.

Economic importance: (1) Circulation of wealth — it prevents concentration of wealth in a few hands; (2) Reduces poverty and inequality by transferring wealth from the rich to the poor; (3) Discourages hoarding — idle wealth decreases each year by 2.5%, so it is invested; (4) Increases investment, production and employment.

(5) Increases demand — the poor spend zakat on necessities, which expands markets; (6) Social security — help for orphans, widows, disabled, unemployed and debtors; (7) Reduces the government's burden of welfare expenditure; (8) Encourages lawful earning and economic stability.

Social importance: purifies wealth and the soul from greed and miserliness; creates brotherhood, love and cooperation between rich and poor; reduces crime, jealousy and class conflict; makes society stable and peaceful; and establishes an Islamic welfare state. In Pakistan zakat and ushr are collected under the Zakat and Ushr Ordinance 1980.
